pages.title: Chemistry, matter, and physical states
printed: -anything that has mass and occupies space
Chemistry is a very broad subject and touches almost every aspect of our lives.
notes: Under Chemistry: “characteristics, composition & transformations”.
Under Matter: “living & non living”; “can be seen & not seen”.
The list is filled with solid, liquid, gas. Plasma and “BE cond” are additional margin notes.
limits: The extra states are learner annotations, not additional completed course lessons in this pilot. No exam permission or timing is inferred from the notes at the top of the page.

pages.title: State, shape, volume, and properties
printed: Various kinds of matter are distinguished by their properties:
a characteristic of a substance that are used in it’s identification and description.
notes: Solid: “definite shape”; “retain volume”.
Liquid: “indefinite shape”; “shape of container”; “Definite volume”.
Gas: “spreads out”; “indefinite shape”; volume “spreads”.
Under What defines physical state?: “Temperature, pressure, internal forces”.
The two property types are filled as physical and chemical.
limits: The table headings and state names are printed; its filled descriptions are handwritten. These are displayed as learner notes rather than an official key.

pages.title: Physical properties and chemical properties
printed: a characteristic of a substance that can be observed without changing the basic identity of the substance
a characteristic of a substance that describes the way the substance undergoes change or resists change.
notes: Examples beside physical properties include color, odor, physical state, melting point, boiling point, and hardness.
Beside chemical properties: “Something is consumed”; “Something is brought to b” (final wording is abbreviated); keywords include flammability, reactivity, decay.
limits: These are the workbook’s printed definitions. The pilot does not silently rewrite them into a different textbook’s wording.

pages.title: Two categories of change
printed: A process that does not alter the basic nature (chemical composition) of a substance.
A process that involves a change in the chemical composition of matter.
notes: “chemical composition is the same”
“H₂O → sol → liq → gas”
“No new substances created”
Beside nail rusting: “Fe → Fe₂O₃”, with “Iron III oxide”.
limits: The handwritten Fe → Fe₂O₃ sketch is preserved as a note, not promoted to a balanced reaction or assessed chemical equation.

pages.title: Observations and the workbook’s change examples
printed: Chemical change always involves at least one of the following
Are the following physical or chemical changes?
notes: The observation list is filled with color change; formation of a solid → a precipitate; formation of a gas → bubbles; temperature → heat is released.
The example classifications in this workbook are handwritten responses. They are not a supplied instructor answer key.
limits: The printed “always” wording is retained. Its scope and the meaning of the observational list need course context or clarification. This pilot does not convert it into an automatic rule that any visible sign proves chemical change.

pages.title: The completed classification map
printed: Anything that has mass and occupies space
Physical combination of 2 or more things
More than one kind of element
notes: The completed boxes read Matter → Pure Substance / Mixture.
Under Pure Substance: Element / Compound. Under Mixture: homogeneous / heterogeneous.
The link between pure substance and mixture is annotated “physical changes”; the element/compound link “chemical changes”.
limits: This is a textual reconstruction of the visible completed tree. The short labels describe branches inside this chart; they are not treated as exhaustive, context-free definitions.

pages.title: Mixtures and a place for clarification
printed: All samples of matter are either pure substances or mixtures.
notes: Beside Mixtures: “physical combination of 2 or more substances.”
Beside Homogeneous: “uniform properties w/ 1 physical state”.
Beside Heterogeneous: “non uniform 1 or more physical state”.
The element note mixes “physical means” and “chemical processes” wording. The compound line is unfilled.
limits: Keep the element wording as an unresolved learner note, rather than silently adopting or correcting it. The incomplete compound line does not become an invented course definition. Use the earlier chart to formulate a question for clarification.

lessons.title: Something can be there without being seen
lessons.short: Matter and the words that identify it
lessons.pre: Seatbelts, everyone. Our first stop is the margin of your own workbook. You wrote that matter can be seen and not seen. Keep that thought beside the printed definition rather than trying to memorize either sentence in isolation. We are looking for the feature that does the identifying—not for how familiar the object looks. The page can stay open while we work.
lessons.question: Which words in the printed definition actually decide whether something is matter? How does your “not seen” note connect to them?
handrails: Find the two requirements joined by “and”. You can copy just those two fragments into your thought.
Separate how you notice something from the feature the definition says it has.
Finish in your own words: “Not seeing it would not settle the question because …”
lessons.post: The first useful anchor is a relationship, not a recital. Your note offers a way into the definition; the definition tells you what your example still has to establish. When we return to the name later, that relationship is what we want waiting behind it.
lessons.change: Write two possible examples of your own. What information would you need before using the definition to classify them?
lessons.return: What short phrase of your own would bring you back to this definition? Keep it beside, not instead of, the source wording.

lessons.title: One table, two questions
lessons.short: Shape and volume without blending them together
lessons.pre: The table has two columns for a reason. Watch what happens when we try to answer both questions with the single word “solid” or “liquid”: we have named the row, but have not yet explained either property. Let the row stay still while we read across it. Your handwritten entries are a record of your thinking, not something you must defend merely because you once wrote them.
lessons.question: Choose one row. What does its shape entry say, and what different information does its volume entry add?
handrails: Read only the shape cell first. What is it describing?
Now read the volume cell. Does your explanation still distinguish the two columns?
Use two short statements: “For shape, my note says … For volume, it says …”
lessons.post: Naming the row and describing what its entries mean are separate accomplishments. A missing label does not erase a useful comparison. Your note about temperature, pressure, and internal forces can stay as a question for a deeper bridge when its course source is available; it need not become an extra memorization demand today.
lessons.change: Move to another row. Which column changes your description, and which parts of your explanation need to stay separate?
lessons.return: Record the contrast you would want to notice next time—not simply the three row names.

lessons.title: An attribute is not yet an event
lessons.pre: Henry points at the page: “Are we saying what it is like, or saying what happened?” That is our entry. Page 3 names characteristics; page 4 names processes. Before the two uses of “physical” and “chemical” blur together, give each noun a job. We are not racing to four labels. We are noticing why the workbook needs four places to put them.
lessons.question: Using the source definitions, explain the difference between describing a property and describing a change. Which part of the wording helps you keep them apart?
handrails: On page 3, locate “a characteristic”. On page 4, locate “A process”.
Choose one example written on page 3. What does it describe about the substance?
Compare it with one process printed on page 4. What is being described as happening?
lessons.post: A label can look nearly identical while its grammatical job changes the question. That is a useful memory anchor for you: keep the characteristic/process distinction, then attach the physical/chemical distinction. You can inspect the exact wording again whenever the two layers collide.
lessons.change: Choose a page-3 example and a page-4 example. Put a reason beside each, without making either explanation longer than two sentences.
lessons.return: Which pair of names is most likely to swap places in your head? Write the distinction you would use to recover them.

lessons.title: What changed—and what stayed itself?
lessons.short: Reason from composition, not just the verb
lessons.pre: Kàra notices how dramatic “burning” sounds beside “melting”. Ms. Luminara keeps a finger on the definition: “The drama is not our criterion. What does the sentence ask us to inspect?” The workbook puts the two definitions next to processes you already recognize. Let us use that familiarity to locate the reason, rather than turn the list into eleven unrelated facts.
lessons.question: Choose one physical-change example and one chemical-change example from your completed list. How would you connect each to the page-4 definition?
handrails: Begin with your annotation as a starting answer, not as proof.
Point to the phrase about chemical composition. What would you need to establish in your chosen example?
Describe what you think stays the same or changes; then give the category a name.
lessons.post: The useful part is the path from the example to the definition. The “Change detective” activity retains the classifications visible in your notes, but compares your thinking with those notes rather than declaring that handwriting is an official key. There is room to revise, mark uncertainty, and bring an unresolved example back to discussion.
lessons.change: Compare “Taking a bite of food” with “Digesting food” from the same page. What makes the question about one process different from the question about the other?
lessons.return: Keep one example that helps you remember the distinction, together with the reason it helps.

lessons.title: Do not jump to the leaves
lessons.short: Read classification as a route through a tree
lessons.pre: Our classification tree has a quiet rule: where you came from matters. “More than one kind of element” sits under a parent branch; it is not a free-floating definition to apply everywhere. Start at the top, then travel one fork at a time. The route gives the short label its context. This is a place where seeing the relationship can do more work than repeating the leaf names.
lessons.question: Choose a leaf on the completed chart. Trace its route from matter, and say what each printed description contributes along the way.
handrails: Read the parent box before the leaf you chose.
Use the printed branch descriptors exactly first; the box names are handwritten.
Now say the route in your own words. What context would vanish if you copied only the last descriptor?
lessons.post: A path through this chart is not a universal substitute for a full definition. It is a useful local structure to learn from. We keep that distinction visible, particularly where the next page leaves a line incomplete. Your understanding can have a clear route even while the wording still needs a question mark.
lessons.change: Choose a leaf on the other side of the first fork. Where does your explanation first have to change?
lessons.return: Which parent branch must you remember when using your chosen short descriptor?

lessons.title: A margin is allowed to hold a question
lessons.short: Preserve an uncertain note without turning it into a rule
lessons.pre: Ástríðr sets two pages side by side. “We can keep what you wrote and still ask what you meant.” The observation list on page 5, the element wording on page 7, and the blank compound line deserve that space. Our job is not to secretly replace your notes with a smoother textbook paragraph. It is to identify what is settled by the available source and what needs its missing context.
lessons.question: Choose one marked uncertainty. What exactly would you ask the instructor or look for in the next source to clarify it?
handrails: Quote the small piece of wording that leaves you uncertain.
Place the related definition or chart descriptor beside it.
Ask a narrow question: “Does this mean … in this setting, or …?”
lessons.post: A clarification question is a useful study result. We have not made a correction merely by noticing a tension. Keeping the evidence, your earlier note, and your current interpretation separate makes a later correction recoverable rather than erasing the path by which you learned it.
lessons.change: Does the answer require a better definition, an example with more context, a complete equation, or confirmation of a course convention?
lessons.return: Save your question to the notebook. It remains unresolved until you add the source or explanation that resolves it.
